next_steps: Redwood to share PrivateLink reference diagram and egress IP playbook
Customer to send VPC CIDR + shared-services peering constraints by 2026-03-12
Schedule hands-on networking workshop with Southbridge infra team (Tom + Jared) week of 3/23
action_items: Aisha: send pricing ballpark for Dedicated vs Private incl reserved burst options (due 2026-03-10)
Tom: prepare PrivateLink design doc and example route table entries (due 2026-03-11)
Jared: provide current NAT/egress architecture and list of external services requiring fixed IPs (due 2026-03-12)
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-03-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Aisha Khan (Redwood AE), Tom Reynolds (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Southbridge Head of Platform), Jared Cole (Lead Infra Eng), Sonia Ruiz (Security), Victor Huang (Cloud Architect)
summary: Discovery to map Southbridge's private connectivity constraints for Redwood Private. Main topics: PrivateLink vs VPC peering, egress IP requirements, region gating, audit/KMS requirements, and a pilot checklist. Customer has shared-services VPC, strict egress IP needs for 3rd-party vendors, SOC2 controls, and a preference to avoid internet egress for inference traffic. Action: share design docs and schedule deeper workshop.
transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Aisha with Redwood, I'll kick us off. Quick intros?
[00:08] Maya: Maya Patel, Head of Platform at Southbridge, we run infra for the payments team.
[00:13] Jared: Jared Cole, I own networks and infra — looking at onramp for LLM inference.
[00:18] Sonia: Sonia Ruiz, security — SOC2 and data residency questions.
[00:22] Victor: Victor Huang, cloud architect, will help with peering and VPC layout.
[00:27] Tom: Hi all, Tom Reynolds on the SE side, focus on networking and deployment architecture.
[00:30] Aisha: Awesome. High level — Southbridge is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, today we want to map the Private option and egress constraints.
[00:42] Maya: Yes, we prefer Private because of PCI scope concerns. We have a shared-services VPC that brokers all egress through NAT stacks and some fixed egress IPs for vendors.
[00:54] Jared: Quick clarifier — when you say fixed IPs, we mean a small set of public IPs that external partners allowlist, so any service we put behind Redwood needs to come from those IPs or be proxied.
[01:06] Tom: Got it. There are two main patterns: VPC peering/cross-account peering into Redwood-hosted VPCs, or PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink-style endpoints) with interface endpoints. Each has different routing and DNS implications.
[01:24] Sonia: From security we want minimal cross-account route table modifications. PrivateLink looks appealing because it keeps traffic off the public internet, and the endpoint is in our account.
[01:35] Aisha: Exactly. One question — do you run an internal shared-services proxy or egress firewall that rewrites IPs?
[01:42] Victor: We do a centralized egress NGW (NAT gateway cluster) in the shared-services VPC. It's a mix of public NAT and some fixed-proxy boxes for specific partners.
[01:53] Tom: Two follow-ups: 1) how many external partners require static IPs? 2) latency sensitivity for inference calls?
[02:00] Maya: About five partners need allowlisting. Latency: interactive chat features — we need p95 generation around 250-400ms for short prompts, long-tail can be higher. Cost is also a factor; we don't want excessive egress charges.
[02:16] Jared: Also, we have multiple AWS accounts and two regions: us-east-1 as primary, eu-west-1 for EU data. We want model hosting in the same region as data to avoid cross-region egress.
[02:31] Tom: Okay, regional placement matters. For Private deployments, you can pick Redwood Private in us-east-1 and eu-west-1; we can keep traffic local. But cross-region fallbacks are an option.
[02:42] Aisha: One nuance — our Private offering integrates with customer-managed PrivateLink endpoints or peering depending on preference. Tom, maybe walk through the PrivateLink flow?
[02:51] Tom: Sure. If we do PrivateLink, Redwood will publish a service name, you create an interface endpoint in your account(s). That endpoint maps to ENIs in the Redwood Private VPC, and traffic stays inside the AWS fabric. From your side you control route tables and security groups. DNS can be configured to resolve the API host to the interface endpoint IP.
[03:14] Victor: How do you handle cross-account IAM for PrivateLink? We avoid wide-open SG rules.
[03:20] Tom: It works via endpoint policy and SGs — you can limit it by principals and security groups. We typically recommend an endpoint policy that restricts to certain services and an SG that only permits the platform CIDRs.
[03:32] Sonia: Auditability — will calls produce traceable logs and access logs for compliance? We need to tie requests back to user principals.
[03:39] Tom: Yes, Redwood can send audit events to your SIEM via a private logging collector or ship logs into your S3 over VPC endpoint with KMS encryption. We also support token-level logging in the Console (configurable retention).
[03:54] Aisha: Side note: we integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping so model payloads keys can be customer-managed.
[03:59] Sonia: That's important — we can't have Redwood-managed keys for certain datasets. KMS integration detail later.
[04:05] Maya: Back to egress — PrivateLink keeps inbound traffic private, but what about outbound calls from the model to third parties? Any model we host might need to call out (webhooks, file fetches) — how do you manage that?
[04:18] Tom: By default, outbound egress from Redwood Private VPC goes through your egress pipeline. We allow two patterns: 1) route outbound via your NAT in shared-services (we peer/route to your NAT) or 2) we maintain egress through Redwood with static egress IP blocks that you can allowlist. Option 1 gives you full control but needs peering/VPC routing; option 2 is simpler but requires trust and we provide IP ranges and SLA.
[04:45] Jared: Option 1 sounds preferable — we want traffic to appear from our NATs. But peering cross-account can get messy with route table propagation. Do you support Transit Gateway attachments?
[04:56] Tom: Yes, we support Transit Gateway and cross-account TGW attachments for scale. For smaller setups, peering works. We can also do AWS RAM share for the endpoint. We'll include a diagram in the doc.
[05:08] Aisha: Quick question on IPs — if we choose Redwood egress IPs, how many IPs do you provide and are they shared across customers?
[05:16] Tom: We provide a small pool per tenant when requested — typically a /29 for predictable allowlisting, but it depends on throughput. IPs are not overlapped with other customers in the same allocation.
[05:26] Maya: /29 might be tight if we have high concurrency, but it's okay as a starting point.
[05:31] Sonia: We also need to support internal-only DNS names and mTLS to partners. Can Redwood support mutual TLS between your egress layer and external partners?
[05:41] Tom: We can support mTLS; that would typically terminate at a customer-managed proxy in your account, or we can terminate in Redwood if you share certs via ACM import or bring-your-own cert process. We should align on cert rotation policies.
[05:54] Victor: What about network segmentation — can we restrict certain models to dedicated subnets or NICs?
[06:00] Tom: Yes, for Dedicated-style capacity we can pin to isolated subnets and provide VLAN-like isolation. For Private, we instantiate per-tenant ENI groups; you get control over SGs on the interface endpoints.
[06:12] Aisha: Let's talk DNS — you mentioned internal resolution to interface endpoints, any gotchas?
[06:18] Tom: If you enable DNS override, your internal hostnames resolve to the interface endpoint. Caveat: clients need to trust the cert SANs; we use the same hostname, just different A records. Split-horizon DNS can be used if you also want outside access.
[06:32] Maya: Okay, region gating — we must ensure EU data stays in eu-west-1, no cross-region training or inference. Are there automated controls to prevent routing to us-east from EU traffic?
[06:45] Tom: You can pin model versions and tenant configs to specific regions. Also routing policies at the API layer will prefer same-region endpoints and we can block cross-region fallbacks if required in policy. We'll note that cross-region fallbacks are off by default for compliance-sensitive tenants.
[07:00] Jared: That helps. A thought on CIDR — our account uses 10.0.0.0/16 widely, some of your sample VPCs in docs use overlapping ranges and cause peering conflicts. Do you have a recommended non-overlapping CIDR plan?
[07:12] Tom: We recommend using /16 clusters like 100.64.0.0/10 or using 172.20.0.0/16 ranges to avoid 10.x overlap. We'll include a recommended CIDR plan with offsets per region.
[07:24] Sonia: On compliance, SOC2 and ISO — do you provide SOC2 Type II and can we bring in an external auditor?
[07:31] Aisha: Redwood has SOC2 Type II, and for Private we provide audit artifacts and allow auditor access under NDA. We'll attach our compliance whitepaper.
[07:40] Sonia: Good. Also need SAML/SSO integration and role-based access control so we can map principals to teams.
[07:47] Tom: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning; RBAC can be synchronized with your identity provider.
[07:54] Maya: Conversation pivot — performance. For our payments flows, p95 under 400ms is desired. If we host models in eu-west for EU traffic, what are realistic token latencies for small-ish models?
[08:06] Tom: For modern Llama-family quantized models on dedicated GPU pools, typical p50 50–120ms, p95 200–400ms depending on sequence length and batching. We'll share benchmark tables.
[08:18] Jared: Do you do KV cache sharing or prefix caching that could affect latency?
[08:23] Tom: Yes, we support KV cache reuse for conversational contexts to reduce token work. Caching is configurable per route so you can tradeoff cost for latency.
[08:33] Aisha: Moving back to networking specifics — Victor, you mentioned you prefer no route table changes in production. That favors PrivateLink right?
[08:41] Victor: Yes, PrivateLink is less invasive. But we have an ops constraint: interface endpoints multiply across accounts and subnets; we need a manageable scale.
[08:50] Tom: We can centralize endpoints in the shared-services VPC and then route from other accounts via TGW to that VPC — that reduces endpoint sprawl. We'll diagram a TGW+central-endpoint design.
[09:02] Maya: About data flow for requests — our app will proxy requests through internal API gateways. Would you recommend connecting those gateways directly to the interface endpoint?
[09:11] Tom: Yes, we typically suggest placing the interface endpoint in the same subnet as your gateway for minimal hop count. Also use internal ALBs if you require internal load balancing before the endpoint.
[09:21] Sonia: Audit trail again — can we have per-request headers signed with user id so the request can be audited across systems?
[09:27] Tom: You can add X-User headers and we capture them in our audit logs; for stronger guarantees we support signed JWTs from your identity provider.
[09:36] Victor: One operational concern — when the Redwood control plane rolls out updates, do you require inbound control connections from our side? We restrict inbound rules tightly.
[09:44] Tom: The control plane communicates via the PrivateLink or peering path — no inbound hole in your public firewall needed. For some metrics/health we may ask for egress to Redwood collectors but those can go through your NAT.
[09:58] Aisha: Let's surface one potential objection: cost. Private connectivity and dedicated pools add cost versus Hosted. How do you present that tradeoff?
[10:06] Tom: We present three levers: Dedicated capacity pricing (commitments lower unit cost), PrivateLink/peering overheads (networking), and caching/batching optimizations to reduce token spend. We also run model recommendations to pick a cheaper compatible model with acceptable quality.
[10:22] Maya: On pilot scoping — we want to run a week-long test in eu-west using a medium-size model with our sample prompts, and we need fixed egress IPs for partner allowlisting. What's the minimum setup?
[10:33] Tom: Minimum: a PrivateLink endpoint in eu-west in your shared-services VPC, a route to your NAT for any outbound calls, and a small Dedicated capacity pool or Private tenant on Redwood in eu-west pinned to your region. We can provision a /29 egress block for allowlist too.
[10:50] Jared: Who creates the interface endpoint — us or Redwood?
[10:54] Tom: Customer creates the endpoint in their account; Redwood provides the service name and policy. We can guide you and send CloudFormation/terraform snippets.
[11:03] Sonia: For the pilot, we also need a security review — can you share your penetration test reports and a high level of data flows?
[11:10] Aisha: Yes, we'll include our pen test summary and flow diagram; for deeper audits we'll set up an NDA and a workbook.
[11:20] Victor: A small nit: DNS TTLs. We need low TTL for failover when switching endpoints. Can you set low TTLs for your hostnames?
[11:28] Tom: TTLs can be set to 30s for internal endpoints; public hostnames we keep reasonable. We'll document exact TTL behavior.
[11:36] Maya: Any constraints on number of concurrent connections per endpoint? We expect bursts during batch job runs.
[11:42] Tom: Interface endpoints scale per ENI capacity; we can size subnets and endpoint ENIs based on expected concurrency. For very high throughput we recommend Transit Gateway + NLB pattern.
[11:55] Jared: About firewalling — do you support outbound domain allowlisting instead of IPs? Some partners only permit domain-based rules.
[12:03] Tom: We can support both. For high-security partners we recommend IP allowlisting. For domain-based rules, egress proxies or resolver policies can translate domains to IPs, but it's less stable.
[12:16] Aisha: Time check — we have about half the call left. Any other big risk areas?
[12:22] Sonia: Data residency and in-flight encryption — are payloads encrypted end-to-end?
[12:27] Tom: Yes TLS for in-flight; at rest we support customer-managed KMS keys for S3 and disk encryption. We can also do envelope encryption on request payloads if needed.
[12:36] Maya: Incident response — in the event of a data incident, what's the escalation path?
[12:41] Aisha: We have a 24/7 on-call for security incidents, and for enterprise customers we provide a dedicated CSM and incident runbook. We'll share SLAs.
[12:49] Victor: If we elect peering instead of PrivateLink, will you accept route propagation from our TGW to yours?
[12:57] Tom: We do TGW attachments and can propagate routes; we'll coordinate on prefix filters and not propagate everything by default.
[13:07] Jared: A practical question — who handles cert rotation for mTLS if we terminate at Redwood?
[13:12] Tom: If Redwood terminates, we can rotate using ACM import or automatic renewals. For customer-terminated, rotation is in your control. We'll recommend short cert lifetimes with automation hooks.
[13:24] Maya: I want clarity on the 'no public internet' promise — is PrivateLink truly preventing any traffic hitting internet?
[13:31] Tom: For inbound API calls via PrivateLink, yes traffic remains within AWS backbone. For outbound calls, if you route via your NAT or TGW, it stays internal until your NAT egress. If you choose Redwood managed egress, those egress hops might traverse Redwood edge but still be from static egress IPs — not public-hosted addresses.
[13:52] Sonia: Will there be egress logs for every outbound connection from the model? We need that for vendor audits.
[13:59] Tom: Yes, we can capture egress connection logs and export them to your logging endpoint over the PrivateLink path.
[14:07] Aisha: There's been mention of shared-services VPC and central endpoints, can you sketch a minimal diagram in the follow-up?
[14:14] Tom: Absolutely — I'll include central-endpoint + TGW diagram plus a peering fallback. Also include terraform snippets for endpoint creation and SG examples.
[14:25] Maya: On the contract side, what's the minimal commitment and SLA for Private?
[14:30] Aisha: For Private we typically do a 6–12 month term for pilots with an option to convert to reserved Dedicated capacity for better pricing. SLA depends on tier; we'll include the enterprise SLA in the doc.
[14:40] Victor: When on-premises or hybrid — do you support air-gapped or on-prem packages?
[14:46] Tom: We have a Private on-prem option for highly regulated customers; it comes as a managed package with air-gapped deployment patterns, though it's heavier to set up. We'll scope that separately if needed.
[14:58] Jared: One more operational ask — blue-green deploys for model rollouts. Can we pin traffic to a model version and rollback automatically if quality drops?
[15:06] Tom: Yes, Redwood has rollout controls — canary percentage, A/B, automatic fallback. Those are exposed in the Console and via API.
[15:16] Sonia: For the pilot, we need to ensure tokens and sample prompts are sanitized. Any guardrails?
[15:22] Tom: We support a data scrubber pre-send and post-hoc monitoring. For highly sensitive inputs we advise customer-side preprocessing.
[15:31] Aisha: Ok let's go through a short recap and then open the floor for any other Qs. Recap: PrivateLink recommended to minimize route table changes, TGW central endpoint to reduce sprawl, two egress patterns (customer NAT vs Redwood egress IPs), KMS integration possible, SOC2 artifacts and pen-test summary will be shared, pilot in eu-west with /29 egress or NAT routing.
[15:54] Maya: That matches our notes. Two additions — we'll review cost delta and provide the CIDR plan.
[16:01] Aisha: Great. Any last questions?
[16:05] Victor: One tiny one — is there a rate limit per endpoint? We want to ensure burst traffic doesn't get throttled unexpectedly.
[16:12] Tom: We set soft rate limits by default but they can be increased via capacity planning. For the pilot we'll provision higher soft limits and monitor.
[16:23] Jared: For the workshop, will Tom lead the networking steps?
[16:27] Tom: Yes, I'll run the hands-on with Jared and Victor.
[16:31] Sonia: From security side I'll review the docs and confirm KMS/cert rotation expectations.
[16:36] Aisha: Perfect. We'll follow up with the design doc, Terraform snippet, pen test summary, pricing ballpark, and a calendar invite for the week of 3/23.
[16:47] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[16:49] Aisha: Thanks all — talk soon.
[16:52] End of recording (approx).
